query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-coating tungsten particles or ligaments with a nanoscale nickel (Ni) interlayer during composite processing will suppress phase separation and interfacial void formation by promoting enhanced interdiffusion and bonding between the W and Cu phases.
generation.material_initial_state: W–Cu composite with discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix, which under current conditions exhibit phase separation and void formation.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin Ni interlayer onto the W surfaces prior to composite consolidation.
generation.conditions: Processing during composite consolidation (e.g., sintering under controlled atmosphere) and service conditions involving elevated heat-transfer and irradiation stresses relevant to plasma-facing/cooling component joints.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanoscale Ni layer at the W–Cu interface.
generation.mechanism: The Ni interlayer acts to improve wettability and interfacial bonding by forming a graded interface during sintering. This promotes interdiffusion between W and Cu, stabilizing the microstructure against phase separation and reducing the propensity for void formation when subjected to operational heat transfer and irradiation conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Ni-coated composite will show improved thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite, with a microstructure that demonstrates reduced phase separation and fewer interfacial voids.
generation.baseline: Untreated W–Cu composites showing significant phase separation and interfacial void formation under similar processing and service conditions.
generation.boundary: This approach is applicable only where Ni coating can be reliably applied without adversely affecting overall composite integrity and where sintering parameters support beneficial interdiffusion, under the specific heat-transfer and irradiation conditions of plasma-facing and cooling components.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal thickness of the Ni interlayer and its long-term stability under high irradiation remain uncertain; scalability of the coating process for industrial fabrication requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composites: one with tungsten pre-coated with a controlled nanoscale Ni layer and one untreated. Subject both sets to accelerated sintering and service simulation tests incorporating combined heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to plasma-facing joints.
measurements: High-resolution SEM/TEM to evaluate interfacial microstructure and presence of voids
X-ray diffraction (XRD) to analyze phase composition and interdiffusion profiles
Steady-state and transient thermal conductivity measurements
Irradiation damage assessment using appropriate spectroscopic techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated composites do not exhibit statistically significant improvement in thermal conductivity and/or if similar levels of phase separation and void formation are observed compared to untreated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.
